youtube.baslik: Communication Approaches for Children with Hearing Loss | Lesson 265 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
Which communication options are offered to the family of a child with hearing loss? In this lesson we take a neutral look at auditory-verbal therapy, auditory-oral approaches, total communication, Turkish Sign Language and the bilingual approach, with their evidence and the decision process.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Joint Committee on Infant Hearing, Year 2019 Position Statement, J Early Hear Detect Interv (2019); AG Bell Academy for Listening and Spoken Language, Principles of LSLS Auditory-Verbal Therapy; Estabrooks, MacIver-Lux and Rhoades, Auditory-Verbal Therapy: Science, Research, and Practice; Brennan-Jones et al., Auditory-verbal therapy for promoting spoken language development in children with permanent hearing impairments, Cochrane Database Syst Rev (2014); Mitchell and Karchmer, Chasing the mythical ten percent, Sign Lang Stud (2004); Law No. 5378 on Persons with Disabilities, Türkiye; Regulation on the Procedures and Principles for Establishing and Implementing the Turkish Sign Language System, Türkiye (2006).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: *Communication* approaches for children with hearing loss
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the communication approaches offered to families of children with hearing loss and the principles behind each.
We will take a neutral look at auditory-verbal therapy, total communication, Turkish Sign Language and the bilingual approach.

maddeler.metin: Language channel: hearing, vision or both
No access to language: developmental risk

cumleler: The shared goal of all communication approaches is for the child to acquire a fully accessible language in the first years of life.
The approaches differ by the channel through which this language is offered: through hearing, through vision, or both.
If a child cannot access a language well through either hearing or vision, language and cognitive development can be seriously affected.
So the heart of the debate is not the method, but the child's access to language.
Choosing an approach is the decision of a family informed about all the options.

cumleler.yazi: The 2019 position statement of the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing also recommends giving families neutral information about all options.
cumleler.ses: The twenty nineteen position statement of the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing also recommends giving families neutral information about all options.

cumleler: Auditory-verbal therapy uses listening as the main channel and guides the family through coaching.
Auditory-oral approaches use listening together with visual cues such as speechreading.
In cued speech, handshapes near the mouth help tell apart sounds that look the same on the lips.
Total communication advocates using all channels together, such as speech, signs, gestures and writing.
In the bilingual approach, the child acquires sign language together with the community's spoken or written language.
These approaches have no sharp borders; many families combine different approaches over time.

cumleler.yazi: Auditory-verbal therapy, or AVT, aims for the child to acquire spoken language mainly through listening.
cumleler.ses: Auditory-verbal therapy, or A V T, aims for the child to acquire spoken language mainly through listening.

cumleler: The prerequisite is making speech audible early and all day with a hearing aid or cochlear implant.
The parent also attends sessions; the therapist acts as a coach working with the parent rather than with the child alone.
The aim is for the parent to apply the strategies learned in sessions at every moment of the day at home.
The therapist usually sits beside the child, so the child turns to taking in speech through the ear rather than the lips.
Certified specialists in this field follow ten principles set by the academy of the Alexander Graham Bell Association.
The long-term goal is for the child to be educated in the same school and class as hearing peers.
The first two principles stress early diagnosis, prompt audiological management and suitable technology.
The next principles aim for the child to use hearing as the main sense for development.
Parents are guided to become the main facilitators of the child's listening and spoken language development.
Listening is built into daily routines such as meals, bath time and play.
The work follows the natural order of listening, speech and language development in hearing children.
Regular formal and informal assessments guide the plan and progress; the last principle is inclusion in mainstream education.

maddeler.metin: All channels: speech, sign, gesture, writing
Often speech and sign at once

cumleler: Total communication is less a method than a philosophy of using every channel that reaches the child.
In practice speech and signs are often used at the same time; this is also called simultaneous communication.
In that case signs usually follow the word order of the spoken sentence; in Türkiye, this is not the grammar of Turkish Sign Language.
Producing speech and sign at the same time can lead to one of the two languages being presented incompletely or distorted.
The strength of the approach is its flexibility; its weakness is the difficulty of building a consistent language model at home and school.
For some children with additional needs, using several channels together can make communication easier.

cumleler.yazi: Turkish Sign Language, or TID, is a full visual language with its own vocabulary and grammar.
cumleler.ses: Turkish Sign Language, or T I D, is a full visual language with its own vocabulary and grammar.

cumleler: Signs are not made of handshapes alone; the location and movement of the hand and where the sign is placed in space also carry meaning.
Facial expressions such as eyebrow and head movements carry grammatical information, such as questions or negation.
Sign languages are not universal; Turkish Sign Language and American Sign Language, for example, are different languages.
Turkish Sign Language is the language of the Deaf community in Türkiye and part of the community's cultural identity.

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, Law No. 5378 on Persons with Disabilities requires a Turkish sign language system for deaf people's education and communication.
cumleler.ses: In Türkiye, Law No. fifty three seventy eight on Persons with Disabilities requires a Turkish sign language system for deaf people's education and communication.

cumleler.yazi: The regulation based on this law was published in 2006; we will look at Deaf culture separately in a later lesson.
cumleler.ses: The regulation based on this law was published in two thousand six; we will look at Deaf culture separately in a later lesson.

maddeler.metin: Most children are born to hearing parents
The family learns sign language too

cumleler: In the bilingual approach, sign language is treated as the child's first language, fully accessible through vision.
The spoken language, Turkish in Türkiye, is taught as a second language in written form, or spoken form if technology supports it.

cumleler.yazi: According to US data, more than 90 percent of children with hearing loss are born to hearing parents.
cumleler.ses: According to U S data, more than 90 percent of children with hearing loss are born to hearing parents.

cumleler: So the bilingual approach requires the family to learn sign language too, a process that takes time and support.
Meeting Deaf adults and the Deaf community gives the family language models and a different perspective.
Some families use sign language along with a cochlear implant, so the child can access both languages.
Randomized trials directly comparing communication approaches are not possible, because the choice belongs to the family.

cumleler.yazi: For example, a 2014 Cochrane review found no studies of auditory-verbal therapy that met its criteria.
cumleler.ses: For example, a twenty fourteen Cochrane review found no studies of auditory-verbal therapy that met its criteria.

cumleler: The existing observational studies show that children's outcomes vary over a very wide range in every approach.
Comparing approaches is hard because family resources, involvement and the child's additional needs affect outcomes.
The common finding of studies is that early and full access to language is decisive, whatever the channel.
So no approach guarantees success; language development should be monitored regularly in every child.
The first factor is how far hearing technology makes speech audible.
The age at which diagnosis and technology begin also sets the timing of access to language.
The language spoken at home, the family's culture, values and expectations are at the center of the choice.
For a child with additional needs, an approach that uses several channels may be more suitable.
If there are Deaf members in the family, sign language may already be the language of the home.
Whether there is a specialist therapist, an education program or a sign language course nearby is also a realistic factor.
The process starts by explaining all the options clearly and neutrally; written information is also given.
Then the family's values, goals and resources are heard; the family is given time to decide.
The chosen approach starts right away; whichever path is chosen, the child's access to language is not delayed.
Language development is measured at regular intervals with age-appropriate scales.
If the child is not making the expected progress, the team and family review the approach; changing path is not a failure.
The audiologist's task is to make sure the child gets the best use of hearing technology, whichever approach is chosen.
The audiologist presents current evidence and the strengths and weaknesses of each approach, not personal preference.
Language that presents sign language as a failure or a last resort misleads the family and disrespects the Deaf community.
When needed, the family is referred to auditory-verbal therapists, special education services, sign language courses and Deaf associations.
That way the family makes its choice based on broad information, not a single opinion.

sahneler.metin: When explaining options, do not say 'sign language if it fails'. Present every path with equal seriousness and stress that the first goal is early, full access to a language.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when explaining the options, do not present sign language as a path to fall back on after failure.
Present each approach with the same seriousness and answer the family's questions without judgment.
At the end of the visit, stress the first goal again: the child's early and full access to a language.
Record the family's decision and schedule the next visit to monitor language development right away.

maddeler.metin: Shared goal: early, full language access
TID: a full language with grammar

cumleler: The shared goal of all communication approaches is the child's early and full access to a language.
Auditory-verbal therapy uses listening as the main channel and guides the parent through coaching in sessions.
Turkish Sign Language is a full language with its own grammar; total communication and the bilingual approach use vision differently.
The choice belongs to the neutrally informed family; whichever path is chosen, language development is monitored regularly.

sahneler.soru: Which is signing at the same time as speaking?
sahneler.aciklama: In total communication, speech and sign are often used _at the same time_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: making signs that go with every word while speaking is typical practice of which approach?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: total communication.
In this simultaneous communication, signs follow spoken word order; Turkish Sign Language is a separate language with its own grammar.
